column2:
A code-review step flags insecure database queries before merge. A single Claude review call catches an injected test vulnerability in only 80% of runs, and the misses look random rather than systematic. The security team wants detection above 95% while keeping review time near a single call's latency.

Which change best raises detection?

A. Have the reviewer output a confidence score per file and re-review any file scored below 0.7.
B. Set the temperature to 0 so the reviewer behaves identically on every run of the same diff.
C. Run several review calls in parallel on the same diff and flag anything that any run flags.
D. Chain three sequential review passes, each one starting from the previous pass's findings.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is the voting form of parallelization: multiple independent attempts at the same task whose outputs are aggregated — if each run catches a miss-at-random vulnerability 80% of the time, taking the union across several parallel runs pushes detection far past 95% while latency stays near one call because the runs execute simultaneously. Option A gates re-review on self-reported confidence, which says little about a vulnerability the reviewer never noticed. Option B aims at repeatability, and a repeatable miss is still a miss — consistency adds no recall, and models released after Claude Opus 4.6 reject a non-default temperature anyway. Option D triples latency and biases later passes toward confirming what earlier passes found instead of looking independently.

• Building effective agents (Anthropic engineering) — Workflow: Parallelization

column2:
Your multi-agent research system pipes every query through a fixed pipeline: one search subagent, one analysis subagent, and one synthesis subagent, each run exactly once. Simple lookups waste two stages, while multi-domain questions — 'compare the last three years of privacy rulings across two jurisdictions' — fail because the number and type of searches required cannot be known until the query itself is examined.

Which pattern fits this variability?

A. Extend the fixed pipeline to five stages so complex queries receive more search and analysis processing.
B. Orchestrator-workers: a lead model examines each query, delegates the subtasks it needs to workers, and synthesizes the results.
C. Routing: classify queries as simple, medium, or complex and send each class to one of three fixed pipelines sized for that class.
D. Evaluator-optimizer: keep the current pipeline but loop the synthesis stage until an evaluator approves the answer.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B matches the defining trigger for orchestrator-workers: subtasks that cannot be predicted in advance. The orchestrator dynamically decomposes each query, spawns however many search or analysis workers that particular question needs, and synthesizes their results — one search for a lookup, six for a cross-jurisdiction comparison. Option A keeps a predefined decomposition, just a longer one: still wasteful for lookups and still the wrong shape for novel query structures. Option C reduces the waste but each bucket still hides unbounded variety — a 'complex' pipeline is still a fixed pipeline. Option D iterates on synthesis quality when the failure happens upstream: the wrong set of searches was run in the first place, and no amount of re-synthesis recovers missing research.

column2:
Your synthesis subagent drafts research summaries that must satisfy a 10-point editorial rubric. Single-pass drafts fail the rubric 40% of the time even though the rubric is already included in the generation prompt. Separately, you have verified that a Claude call given a draft plus the rubric identifies the specific failing points with high agreement against human editors.

Which pattern best exploits that verified grading ability?

A. Generate five independent drafts in parallel and publish whichever one the grader ranks best.
B. Append the grader's rubric a second time at the end of the generation prompt so that its ten points get more emphasis.
C. Have the drafting model grade its own output and revise until it awards itself a passing score.
D. Loop draft, grade, revise, feeding the grader's critique to the drafter until the rubric passes or a retry cap is hit.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is the evaluator-optimizer pattern — a generator and a distinct evaluator in a feedback loop — and it fits precisely because the two preconditions hold: clear evaluation criteria exist, and iterative refinement demonstrably adds value since the grader pinpoints the exact failing rubric points for the drafter to fix. Option A pays for five full drafts while discarding the grader's most valuable output, its specific critique; selection without refinement can leave you publishing the least-bad failure. Option B is repetition of instructions already present — the prompt-only approach that produced the 40% failure rate. Option C collapses the roles: self-grading is exactly the unreliable self-assessment the verified independent grader exists to replace.

column2:
Your deployment agent edits YAML service configs with a text-editing tool and then reports success. In 12% of runs the resulting file is invalid — an edit landed inside the wrong block, or the file had been changed by another process since the agent last saw it — yet the transcript shows the agent confidently reporting success anyway.

Which TWO changes most improve the agent's reliability? (Select TWO.)

A. Have the agent re-read the file immediately before editing so its edits apply to the current state.
B. Add a system-prompt instruction telling the agent to be extremely careful with YAML structure and indentation.
C. Set the temperature of the editing calls to 0 so the same edit is produced on every run.
D. After each edit, have the agent re-read or lint the file and treat any failure as feedback to fix before reporting success.
column3:
Correct Answer: A and D. Options A and D are environment inspection applied before and after action: an agent cannot assume the effect of its actions, so reading current state before editing eliminates the stale-file failures, and validating after editing converts silent corruption into feedback the agent can act on in-loop — fixing the wrong-block edits instead of reporting success over a broken file. Option B changes no observation the agent makes; a carefully worded prompt still leaves the agent blind to the file's actual state, so the same failures recur politely. Option C targets run-to-run variation, but the failures stem from unobserved state, not variance — the same edit applied to a stale or misread file is wrong every time.

column2:
You are building an assistant for internal developer requests: 'find why this test is flaky,' 'upgrade this dependency and fix the breakage,' 'trace where this config value comes from.' After mapping 40 sample tickets you cannot write a step sequence that covers even half of them — yet all were solvable using file search, file reading, and command execution.

Which architecture fits this workload?

A. An agent that plans its own steps per request, looping over a few general tools — search, read, execute — until done.
B. A routing workflow that classifies each request into one of the 40 mapped types and then runs that type's scripted steps.
C. A chained workflow containing the union of all steps observed across the 40 tickets, executed in a fixed order.
D. A parallelization workflow that runs every candidate step simultaneously and aggregates whichever ones succeed.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is the situation agents exist for: when required steps cannot be predetermined, the model plans dynamically, observes the environment after each action, and composes a small flexible toolset in ways you never enumerated — and the stem confirms the whole workload reduces to a few general capabilities. Option B scripts the past; the mapping already failed to cover half of the observed tickets, and novel request shapes keep arriving. Option C executes mostly irrelevant steps on every request and still breaks the moment a ticket needs an unobserved sequence. Option D parallelizes steps that are inherently dependent — you must find the flaky test before you can fix it — so running everything at once is incoherent for these tasks.

column2:
Your document-processing agent has 22 hyper-specific tools (extract_invoice_date, extract_invoice_total, extract_po_number, and so on). Every new document type triggers a request for three or four more tools, requests that match no existing tool simply fail, and the tool list already consumes 3,500 prompt tokens.

How should the toolset be redesigned?

A. Keep the 22 specialized tools but write richer descriptions so the agent selects the correct one more often.
B. Merge all 22 tools into one extract_field tool whose operation enum lists every supported field.
C. Replace them with a few general, composable tools — such as a document reader plus code execution — the agent can combine.
D. Add a second routing model that inspects each request and pre-selects which of the specialized tools the agent is allowed to call.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C applies the tool-abstraction principle: agents work best with a small set of general tools they can combine in unanticipated ways — the same reason Claude Code ships with bash and file tools rather than a refactor_tool — so generic read-and-compute capabilities cover novel document types without minting a new tool per field. Option A improves selection among existing tools, but the observed failures are coverage gaps — requests with no matching tool — which no description can close. Option B compresses the list without adding capability; the enum still enumerates fields, so novel fields still fail. Option D is an over-engineered routing layer that spends effort choosing among tools that collectively still cannot do the job.

column2:
An invoice-extraction agent your team runs calls a record_invoice tool that your own code executes. On some invoices the handler's validator rejects the call: the JSON in the tool_use block's input parses, but the required vendor_tax_id field is absent. Each affected response has a stop_reason of tool_use and an output token count far below the request's max_tokens. The failures cluster on invoices that print the tax ID only in the page footer.

What should the handler do when it receives one of these calls?

A. Return a tool_result with is_error: true whose content names the missing vendor_tax_id field.
B. Retry the same request with a larger max_tokens value to give the tool call room to finish.
C. Fill vendor_tax_id with a placeholder in code and run the tool with the patched input.
D. Discard the response and re-send the identical request until a call includes vendor_tax_id.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. A stop_reason of tool_use, JSON that parses and token usage well under the cap show that Claude finished the call and left out a required argument. For an invalid call the documented handling is to return a tool_result marked is_error: true that says what is wrong; Claude then reissues the call with the missing value filled in, and here the tax ID is on the invoice to be found. Option B treats the fault as truncation, but nothing was cut off: a larger max_tokens is the remedy when stop_reason is max_tokens and the block is incomplete. Option C writes an invented value into the record. Option D tells Claude nothing about the fault, so each resend is a fresh attempt that can omit the field again while the whole request is paid for a second time.

column2:
A developer new to tool use is building a travel assistant on the Messages API with two tools that their own code runs, get_flight_status and get_gate_info. Their handler was written on the assumption that a response requests one tool. In testing, when a traveler asks about a flight's status and its gate in one message, some responses have a stop_reason of tool_use and contain two tool_use blocks, one per tool, each with its own id. The two lookups do not depend on each other.

How should these responses be handled?

A. Run the first tool_use block, return its tool_result, and call the API to let Claude request the second tool.
B. Retry the identical request until the response comes back with a single tool_use block.
C. Run both tools and return their outputs in one tool_result that carries the first block's id.
D. Run both tool_use blocks and return one tool_result per block in a single user message.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. A response with a stop_reason of tool_use can carry several tool_use blocks, and the API expects one tool_result for each, matched by tool_use_id and sent together in the next user message. Option A is the right loop for a response that requests one tool, but here it leaves the second id unanswered, and the API rejects the follow-up request with a 400 error saying that tool_use ids were found without tool_result blocks. Option C fails the same way: one block answers one id, so the second call still has no result, and two outputs are filed under the wrong call. Option B discards a valid response and spends tokens waiting for a shape Claude is not obliged to produce; calling several tools in one response is default behavior, and these lookups are independent, so both can be run at once.

column2:
An agent loop your team maintains appends each assistant response to its message history with the full content, tool_use blocks included, and returns every tool output as a tool_result block in the following user message. To keep requests small, a helper deletes the oldest messages whenever the history passes 30 messages. In long sessions the API sometimes rejects a request with a 400 error referencing an unknown tool_use_id, and each rejected history begins with a user message made up of tool_result blocks.

What is the fix?

A. Append the assistant response's full content to history before each tool_result is sent.
B. Make the helper cut only where each tool_use message stays with its tool_result message.
C. Strip tool_use_id from the oldest retained results to stop the API from checking them.
D. Raise max_tokens to leave room for the complete history in every request.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. The loop already stores complete assistant content, so the pairing is being broken later: the trimming helper sometimes deletes an assistant message that holds a tool_use block while keeping the user message that answers it. The API requires each tool_result to follow its tool_use in the history it receives, so the orphaned result is rejected, which is why every failing history starts with tool_result blocks. Trimming has to treat a tool call and its result as one unit and drop or keep both. Option A describes what the loop does already and cannot repair a pair that is split afterwards. Option C removes the field that ties a result to its call instead of restoring the call it refers to, so the history is still invalid. Option D confuses the output cap with input size: max_tokens limits what Claude generates and does nothing for a history cut in the wrong place.

column2:
Your research system reviews vendor contracts across four independent dimensions: data privacy, liability, pricing terms, and termination clauses. A single prompt covering all four finds 97% of the labeled issues on a 300-contract eval set, against a 95% target, with no drop-off for the dimensions listed last, and it returns within the reviewers' latency budget. An engineer proposes replacing it with four specialized calls, one per dimension, on the grounds that parallelization is the standard pattern for independent subtasks.

Which response to the proposal is best supported?

A. Adopt sectioning with four parallel calls, one per dimension, and aggregate the findings.
B. Keep the single call as it is, and use the 300-contract eval to judge any later proposal to split it.
C. Keep the single prompt, but run it three times per contract and merge the issues that the runs find.
D. Chain four calls, one dimension at a time, and carry each call's findings forward to the next.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. Sectioning earns its extra calls when one prompt demonstrably loses focus across independent subtasks, and the measurements here say it does not: recall is above target, the later dimensions are not neglected, and latency is within budget. Anthropic's guidance is to use the simplest design that meets the requirement and to add complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes. Option A would quadruple the calls and add aggregation logic to fix a problem the eval does not show. Option C is voting under another name: it triples the cost to average out random misses that nobody has observed. Option D adds four calls of sequential latency and passes findings between dimensions that are independent of one another. If a later eval shows a dimension being missed, the call can be split at that point, with the existing eval as the baseline for judging the change.

column2:
A code-review step flags insecure database queries before merge. On an eval of 50 injected test vulnerabilities, a single Claude review call catches 40. The 10 misses are not random: each one builds its SQL through an internal helper, raw_fragment(), and 20 repeat runs on each of those diffs never produced a flag, while the other 40 cases are caught on every run. The review prompt's sole instruction is 'flag insecure database queries'. The security team wants detection above 95% at about a single call's latency.

Which change best raises detection?

A. Add an explicit criterion to the prompt, with a code example, for SQL built through that helper.
B. Run several review calls in parallel on the same diff and flag anything that any run flags.
C. Have the reviewer report a confidence score per file and re-review any file that scores below 0.7.
D. Chain three sequential review passes, each one starting from the findings of the pass before it.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. The misses are systematic: the same ten diffs are missed on every one of 20 runs, and all share a pattern the prompt never mentions. A vague instruction such as 'flag insecure database queries' leaves the model to decide what counts, and it does not treat a call to an internal helper as risky; stating the pattern as an explicit criterion, with an example, tells it what to report. Option B is the right tool for misses that vary from run to run, where the union of several runs recovers what one run drops, but here every run misses the same cases, so the union is no larger than a single run. Option C relies on self-reported confidence about code the reviewer did not find suspicious in the first place. Option D triples latency, and each later pass inherits the same blind spot from the same prompt.

column2:
Your synthesis subagent drafts research summaries that must satisfy a 10-point editorial rubric. Single-pass drafts fail the rubric 40% of the time even though the rubric is included in the generation prompt. A teammate has written a grader — a Claude call given a draft plus the rubric — and proposes looping draft, grade and revise until the grader passes each summary. On 100 drafts that human editors have already scored, the grader's pass or fail verdict matches the editors' on 54, and the rubric points it names as failing rarely match theirs.

What should the team do with the proposal?

A. Build the loop as proposed and feed the grader's critique to the drafter until the rubric passes or a retry cap is hit.
B. Generate five drafts per summary in parallel and publish whichever one the grader ranks highest.
C. Rework the grader with explicit criteria per rubric point and re-check it against the editors' scores before looping.
D. Drop the separate grader and have the drafting model score its own output and revise until it passes.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. An evaluator-optimizer loop is only as good as its evaluator: the pattern fits when there are clear evaluation criteria and the grader's feedback is known to be sound. Here the grader agrees with human editors on 54 of 100 drafts, barely better than a coin flip, and blames the wrong rubric points, so its critiques would steer revisions at random. The documented advice for model graders is to give them detailed, explicit rubrics and to test their reliability before relying on them at scale. Option A wires that noise into a loop, where drafts are revised until an unreliable judge happens to pass them. Option B has the same judge choose among five drafts, so the selection is no more trustworthy and costs five times the drafting. Option D replaces a weak grader with self-grading, in which the model reviews its own work with the reasoning that produced it.

column2:
A stakeholder requests a 'multi-agent AI platform' — a coordinator, specialist subagents, and long-term memory — to tag inbound sales emails with one of five categories and a priority level. Your team has built a single classification prompt with a few examples; on the labeled test set it scores 83% against an acceptance bar of 95%, and three rounds of prompt revisions have not moved it. Error analysis shows that nearly all the misses are priority labels, which depend on whether the sender's company holds an active contract — a fact recorded in the CRM and absent from the email text.

Which change is most likely to close the gap?

A. Continue revising the single prompt's wording and examples until the priority labels reach the bar.
B. Build the coordinator and specialist subagents, with one subagent dedicated to priority assignment.
C. Run the single prompt three times per email and take the majority label for category and priority.
D. Add a CRM lookup of the sender's contract status and pass the result to the prompt with each email.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. Starting with one prompt was the right first move, and the eval has now shown where it falls short: priority depends on contract status, which the email does not contain. Prompt work cannot produce a fact that is missing from the input, so the proportionate step is to supply that fact, with a lookup added in front of the same classification call, and then re-score. That adds the one capability the evidence calls for. Option A keeps tuning wording after three revisions made no difference, for the same reason: the information is not there to be read. Option B adds a coordinator, subagents and memory, yet a subagent reasoning over the same email text lacks the same fact. Option C averages out run-to-run variation, but these errors are consistent and caused by absent data, so the majority label is wrong as well.

column2:
Your travel agent's search_flights tool has a detailed description: its purpose, when to use it and when not to, the IATA airport-code input format with an example, and what it returns. In production, 28% of calls fail the tool's input validation. Logs show that Claude selects the tool for flight questions alone and passes a well-formed three-letter IATA code in every failing call; the rejected codes all belong to airports that opened after the validator's hard-coded airport list was last updated.

What is the most effective fix?

A. Expand the tool description with more examples of valid IATA codes and a firmer statement of the format.
B. Add few-shot examples to the system prompt that show correctly formed flight-search calls for common routes.
C. Update the tool's validator to check codes against a current airport source in place of its stale list.
D. Return an error result that tells Claude to resubmit each failing search with a different airport code.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. A tool description is the lever when Claude chooses the wrong tool or forms its arguments badly, and the logs rule both out: Claude calls the tool for the right questions and sends valid IATA codes, and every failure traces to the validator's out-of-date airport list. That is a defect in the tool's own code, and a code change is what fixes it. Option A rewrites a description that is already doing its job; no wording makes the validator accept an airport it does not know. Option B gives the model examples of something it already does correctly. Option D reports a valid call as an input error, which pushes Claude to substitute a different airport and return flights the traveler did not ask for. Reading the logs before changing the prompt is what separates a model-side cause from a tool-side one.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.1

References:
• Define tools — Best practices for tool definitions
• Troubleshooting tool use — Claude calls the wrong tool

column2:
Your operations agent answers 'where is the replacement part for this customer's open repair?' by calling three tools over three sequential assistant turns: find_customer returns a customer ID, get_open_repair takes that ID and returns a part number, and check_inventory takes the part number and returns the warehouse that holds the part. The chain adds about 25 seconds of round-trip latency, the same three calls occur in this order for 60% of requests, and each call needs the previous call's output as its input.

Which change most reduces the number of request-response cycles for this question?

A. Keep parallel tool use enabled and have the handler run every tool_use block in a response before replying.
B. Add a batch tool that accepts a list of the three invocations and executes them in a single round trip.
C. Add a system-prompt instruction that tells Claude to issue all three calls together in one response.
D. Add one tool that takes the customer's details and performs all three lookups in order inside your code.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. The three lookups form a chain: each needs the output of the one before it, so Claude cannot write the second or third call until the earlier result has come back. A single tool that accepts the customer's details and runs the chain in your code turns three model round trips into one, which is the documented reason to consolidate frequently chained steps into one tool. Option A helps when calls are independent, because several tool_use blocks can then arrive in one response; here there is nothing to parallelize. Option B has the same limit: a batch tool still needs every invocation's arguments up front, and two of them do not exist yet. Option C asks for calls whose inputs are unknown, which invites guessed IDs; the parallel tool use guidance is to batch only calls that are independent of each other.

column2:
Your order-management agent defines four action tools: refund, replace, escalate, and request_info. Every request sets tool_choice to {"type": "any"}. Policy says that an order problem is handled through one of the four actions, and that a message the agent can answer from its instructions — store hours, the returns window, a thank-you — gets a plain-text reply. Transcripts show that 15% of customer messages are of that second kind, and on those the agent calls request_info or escalate.

Which change brings the agent in line with the policy?

A. Keep tool_choice at {"type": "any"} and add a system-prompt rule to reply in text to simple questions.
B. Set tool_choice to {"type": "tool", "name": "request_info"} to make clarification the default action.
C. Set tool_choice to {"type": "auto"} and describe in the system prompt when an action is needed.
D. Set tool_choice to {"type": "none"} on every request to make sure simple questions get text replies.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. any obliges Claude to call one of the provided tools on each turn, so a message that needs a sentence in reply still produces an action, here an unnecessary request_info or escalate. The policy has two legitimate outcomes, an action or a text reply, and auto is the setting under which Claude decides between them on each turn; the system prompt steers where that line falls. Option A leaves the forcing in place, and a prompt rule does not let the model answer in text while the request requires a tool call. Option B narrows every response to one tool, which is further from the policy. Option D removes tool calls altogether, so order problems could not be refunded, replaced or escalated. Currency note (Oct 2026): current docs say any and tool return a 400 error on Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, which accept only auto and none.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.3

References:
• Define tools — Forcing tool use
• Tool use with Claude — When Claude uses tools

column2:
An invoice-extraction pipeline instructs Claude in its prompt to 'respond with a JSON object containing vendor, invoice_date and total' and parses the reply with json.loads. Spot checks of the records that parse find their values correct. On 6% of documents, though, parsing fails: the reply opens with a sentence of commentary, contains a trailing comma, or leaves a quotation mark inside a vendor name unescaped. In each failing case the response's stop_reason is end_turn.

Which change most reliably eliminates these failures?

A. Define a record_invoice tool with a strict JSON schema for the three fields and read them from the tool_use input.
B. Clarify each field's definition in the prompt and add checks that compare extracted values with expected answers.
C. Add few-shot examples of well-formed JSON replies and tell Claude to output the object with no other text.
D. Raise max_tokens on each request to give the reply room to close its braces and quotation marks.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. The failures are syntax failures — commentary before the object, a trailing comma, an unescaped quote — in replies that Claude ended normally, which is what free-text JSON produces occasionally however carefully it is prompted. Defining the record as a tool's input schema, with strict mode, moves the structure out of prose: the fields arrive as a schema-valid tool_use input, and json.loads has nothing to choke on. Option B is the remedy for a different fault, values that are well formed but wrong; here the parsed values are already correct. Option C makes malformed replies rarer but leaves the format as a request the model can still miss. Option D addresses truncation, and a stop_reason of end_turn shows these replies were not cut off. Schema enforcement removes syntax errors and nothing more, so value checks still matter for meaning.

Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.3

References:
• Strict tool use — Why strict tool use matters for agents
• Structured outputs — Why use structured outputs

column2:
To cut model costs by 50%, an engineer proposes moving your ticket-triage job to the Message Batches API. Each ticket is handled by a single request: the ticket text goes in, a record_triage tool is defined with a JSON schema for category, priority and summary, and the pipeline reads those fields from the tool_use block of the response. Your code never executes the tool and never sends a tool_result. The triage output feeds a staffing report that is compiled once a week.

Which assessment of the proposal is accurate?

A. It will stall, as a batched request cannot pause for the result that its tool_use block is waiting on.
B. It will work, as the Batches API executes record_triage itself and returns the tool's result per request.
C. It will work only if each ticket is its own batch, as results are otherwise returned in arbitrary order.
D. It will work, as every request finishes in one response and a weekly report tolerates the batch window.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. The limit on batching concerns loops in which your code has to run a tool and return the result before Claude can finish; a batched request cannot do that mid-flight. This job has no such loop: each request ends with a tool_use block whose input is the deliverable, nothing is executed, and no further turn is sent. Tool definitions are supported in batches, and a weekly report sits comfortably inside the up-to-24-hour window, so the discount comes at no functional cost. Option A describes the multi-turn case, which this is not. Option B reaches the right verdict for a false reason: record_triage is a client tool, which only your application could run, and here nothing runs it; each response simply ends with the tool_use block. Option C misreads how results are correlated: one batch holds many requests, each identified by its own custom_id, so result order does not matter and per-ticket batches add overhead for nothing.

• Batch processing — Retrieving batch results

column2:
You submit a Message Batch of 50,000 structured-extraction requests, one per support ticket. Each request carries the ticket ID as its custom_id, and your code writes each result back to the ticket row that its custom_id names. After the batch's processing has ended, QA finds 1,900 ticket rows with no extracted fields. For every one of those tickets the result's type is expired: the batch reached its 24-hour limit before the request was sent to the model. The other 48,100 results are succeeded, and spot checks find their fields on the right tickets.

What is the correct way to complete the extraction?

A. Re-run the write-back and join the downloaded results to the ticket rows on custom_id a second time.
B. Submit a new batch of the 1,900 expired requests, identified by custom_id, with their content unchanged.
C. Submit the full set of 50,000 requests as a new batch and overwrite the rows that were already filled.
D. Split each of the 1,900 tickets into smaller chunks and submit the chunks as a new batch of requests.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. A result of type expired means the batch hit its 24-hour limit before that request reached the model: nothing was generated, nothing was billed, and the request was never rejected as invalid. The remedy is to resubmit just those requests, which the custom_id on each result identifies, with their content as it was. Option A repeats a join that is working; matching on custom_id is the right way to tie results to tickets, but the 1,900 rows are empty because no output exists to join. Option C pays a second time for 48,100 requests that succeeded and puts good rows at risk. Option D is the modification for a request that failed as invalid because its input was too long for the context window; nothing here says the tickets are too long, so chunking alters requests of the same kind as the 48,100 that succeeded and fragments each ticket's extraction for no benefit.

• Batch processing — Batch limitations

column2:
A prompt generates one-day meal plans from each athlete's profile. It already prescribes steps — list the athlete's dietary restrictions, draft the plan, then verify each item against every restriction — and restriction violations have fallen from 20% of plans to 2%. Some of the restrictions are medically diagnosed allergies. Each plan lists its ingredients in a structured field, and the ingredient catalog tags every ingredient with the allergens it contains. The clinical lead requires that no plan containing one of an athlete's listed allergens is ever sent to that athlete.

Which change meets that requirement?

A. Extend the prescribed steps with a second verification pass and a firmer warning about allergy risks.
B. Add few-shot examples of plans in which allergy restrictions interact with training-goal requirements.
C. Check each plan's ingredients against the athlete's allergens in code and return failures for regeneration.
D. Ask the model to rate its confidence that each plan is allergen-free, and hold plans it rates below 0.9.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. Prescribed reasoning steps are instructions, and instructions are followed with high but not perfect reliability, which is what the remaining 2% shows. A requirement that has to hold on every plan, and that can be tested mechanically because ingredients and allergen tags are structured data, belongs in code: a deterministic check blocks any plan that contains a listed allergen, and returning the specific violation lets the model produce a compliant replacement. Option A adds more of the technique that brought the rate down; it may lower the rate further and leaves it above zero. Option B has the same limit, since examples raise the odds of compliance without guaranteeing it. Option D relies on the model's self-reported confidence, which is poorly calibrated, so a plan containing an allergen can be rated 0.95 and sent. The prompt steps are worth keeping, because they reduce how often the check has to reject a plan.

Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.4

References:
• Building effective agents (Anthropic engineering) — Workflow: Prompt chaining
• Reduce hallucinations — Advanced techniques

column2:
Your extraction eval grades every field in code, by exact string match against a labeled expected value, across 2,000 test cases on each prompt change. That works for invoice_number and total, but the free-text issue_summary field fails 58% of test cases. A manual review of 100 of those failures finds that 91 of the summaries state the customer's problem accurately in different words from the reference, so the field's score does not separate good prompt versions from bad ones.

How should grading be restructured?

A. Keep code checks for the exact-value fields and grade issue_summary with a model grader given explicit criteria.
B. Keep all grading in code and replace the exact match on issue_summary with keyword and length rules.
C. Add the reference summaries to the extraction prompt as examples to bring its wording in line with the labeled values.
D. Drop issue_summary from the eval and report scores for the two exact-value fields at each prompt change.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. Exact match is the right grader for fields that have one correct value, and it is fast and reliable there. A summary has many correct wordings, so exact match fails accurate answers, as the manual review of 91 in 100 shows; judging whether two phrasings state the same problem takes a model grader, given a clear rubric and checked against a sample of human judgments before it is trusted across 2,000 cases. Option B swaps one brittle rule for another: keyword and length rules pass summaries that use the right terms and get the problem wrong, and fail accurate paraphrases that use other terms. Option C leaks the test labels into the prompt, so the score would rise on those cases without summaries improving on tickets the eval has not seen. Option D removes the measurement of a field the product depends on.

Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1

References:

• Define success criteria and build evaluations — Tips for LLM-based grading

column2:
A building-inspection firm uses Claude to turn surveyors' site notes into structured defect records. Each record has a measurement_text string and a nullable value_mm number. Surveyors often describe sizes informally — 'crack about a hand's width', 'gap you could fit two fingers in' — and in 18% of those records Claude writes an exact figure into value_mm, such as 101.6 for the hand's width, although the prompt states: 'Do not guess measurements; use null when no exact figure is given.' Notes average 150 words, and records for notes that give exact figures are correct.

What is the root cause, and what should the team change?

A. The numeric field cannot express absence, so the team should make value_mm optional in the schema.
B. The rule is stated without being demonstrated, so the team should add examples of informal notes with correct records.
C. The notes dilute the instruction, so the team should repeat it in capitals immediately before each surveyor's note.
D. The model is guessing under uncertainty, so the team should have it output a confidence score and drop low scores.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. The prompt states the rule in the abstract, and nothing shows the model what following it looks like for a phrase such as 'a hand's width', where a conversion is easy to produce and looks helpful. Few-shot examples that pair informal notes with the correct record — the phrase kept in measurement_text and value_mm set to null — demonstrate the judgment, and the model generalizes it to informal wordings the examples do not list. Option A misreads the schema: value_mm is nullable, so absence can be expressed. Option C treats the failure as an instruction lost in a long input, but the notes average 150 words, and repeating a rule with more emphasis is the weaker lever when a stated rule is not being applied. Option D filters on the model's self-reported confidence, which is poorly calibrated, so a confidently converted 101.6 would pass.

References:

• Increase output consistency — Constrain with examples

column2:
A clinic digitizes handwritten patient-intake forms with Claude. Each request defines a record_intake tool whose schema lists insurance_member_id as a required string, and the pipeline stores the tool_use input. An audit of 400 records for self-pay patients, whose forms leave the insurance section blank, finds a well-formed member ID in 37 of them and an empty string or 'N/A' in the rest; none of the 37 IDs exists in any insurer's system. Records for insured patients match their forms. The prompt already says 'extract only what is written on the form'.

What is the most likely root cause of the invented IDs?

A. The schema makes the field a required string, with no null or 'not present' value to return for a blank ID.
B. The tool description is too brief for the model to tell which section of the form holds the member ID.
C. The handwriting on self-pay forms is harder to read and leads the model to misread digits in the ID.
D. The prompt's instruction is worded too mildly and sits too early in the prompt for the model to act on it.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. Listing insurance_member_id as a required string tells the model that every record carries a value, so when the insurance section is blank the one way to complete a valid tool call is to supply some string, which is a placeholder in most records and a plausible ID in 37. The repair follows from the cause: make the field nullable and state in its description that null means no ID is written on the form. Option B does not fit the evidence, because records for insured patients match their forms, so the model finds and reads the field when it is there. Option C fails for a similar reason: a blank section has no digits to misread. Option D asks a prompt instruction to outweigh the schema, but the instruction is present and the schema keeps demanding a value, so stronger wording or a different position leaves the conflict in place.

References:

• Reduce hallucinations — Basic hallucination minimization strategies

column2:
A logistics company extracts customs data from shipping manifests with Claude. The extraction tool is defined with strict: true, and no output has failed schema validation in three months. A separate stage checks each record in code — the line weights must sum to the stated gross weight, and the origin and destination ports must differ — and routes about 3% of records to a clerk for correction. To simplify the pipeline, an engineer proposes removing that stage on the grounds that strict mode already guarantees correct output.

What is the best response to the proposal?

A. Accept it, as output that matches the schema on every request has already been validated.
B. Accept it, as a prompt instruction to verify weights and ports gives the same protection at lower cost.
C. Reject it, as strict mode constrains only the structure of each record and leaves its values unchecked.
D. Reject it, as strict mode is known to fail on long manifests and the stage catches those failures.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. Strict mode constrains generation to the tool's JSON schema, so every record has the right fields and types; it has no view of whether a weight was read from the wrong column or one port was entered twice. Those are semantic errors, and the code stage is what catches them: about 3% of schema-valid records fail its checks, and removing it would pass those records on unreviewed. Option A equates matching the schema with being validated, which holds for structure and not for values. Option B replaces a deterministic arithmetic check with a prompt instruction, which the model follows most of the time and not every time. Option D reaches the right decision on a false premise: in three months no output has failed schema validation, and the stage tests sums and ports, not schema conformance.
